To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the motor cortex of female observers is preferentially modulated by physical attributes of observed hand actions.

(1) the passive observation of hand gestures is associated with an increase in motor cortex excitability; (2) the motor cortex is preferentially activated during passive observation of hand movements that are physically similar or dissimilar in terms of skin color and sex with respect to self; and (3) this effect is observed in the right hemisphere of female participants only.
physical similarity with the observed hand modulates motor cortex excitability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms underlying the observation of actions and how self-related factors may modulate the activity within the MNS.
the question of how self-related processes influence the activation of the human mirror neuron network during the observation of hand actions.
the role of self-relatedness in the MNS and the neural mechanisms underlying the perception of body actions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human MNS is modulated by physical similarity between self and an observed body part.
the observation of a hand action that is similar to the self in terms of gender and skin color, increases motor cortex excitatory activity.
the observation of a body part with a physical similarity (i.e. sex and skin color) to the self, increases the excitability of motor cortex.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the MNS is not a unitary system and is modulated by self-relevant properties of the observed action.
the motor cortex is more activated when observing actions performed by someone who looks like us.
physical properties of the observed body part modulates motor cortex excitability in a gender specific manner.
The main takeaway from our work is that
self-representation in the MNS may be more complex than initially thought, and may depend on the physical similarity between an observed hand action and the self.

the human brain is not only sensitive to the social group to which an action belongs, but it also takes into account physical features that make the observed action more similar or dissimilar than the self.
the MNS is not a simple motor system, but a complex system that is modulated by a variety of cognitive processes.
